steps.text:
## Welcome to Papyrus!

This tutorial walks you through the basics in about 4 minutes.

The **Project button (📁)** in the toolbar is your starting point. Click it to create a new project or open an existing one. Every note, highlight, and analysis result lives inside a project file (`.pdfproj`).

## Add your first PDF

With a project open, click the **Project (📁)** button and choose **Add PDF to Project**. You can also drag one or more PDFs directly onto the document list on the left.

Added PDFs appear in the **Document Explorer** — click any document there to open it in the reader.

## The Research dock

This is the **Research Assistant dock** — the heart of Papyrus. It contains seven tabs:

- 💬 **Chat** — ask questions, get answers grounded in your documents
- 💡 **Brainstorm** — generate ideas and arguments
- 🔬 **Analysis** — extract structured knowledge from a PDF
- 🧭 **Research Agent** — autonomous multi-step research
- 🧰 **Custom Tools** — run saved workflows
- 🛠️ **Blueprint Editor** — build and test new workflows
- 🔍 **Search** — local and external academic search

We'll explore these in the dedicated tutorials. Click **Next** to continue.

## Highlights & Notes

While reading a PDF, select any text and right-click to **highlight** it in one of five colours. Add a written note to any highlight.

All your highlights and notes appear in the **Notes dock** (shown here). You can filter by document, tag, or note type.

That's the basics! Explore the other tutorials for in-depth walkthroughs of every feature.

## Step 1 — Import a PDF

Click the **Project (📁)** button and choose **Add PDF to Project**, or drag a PDF file directly onto the document list on the left. Papyrus adds it to the project and opens it in the reader.

If your PDF is scanned (image-only, no selectable text), right-click it in the Document Explorer and choose **Run OCR** first to extract the text.

## Step 2 — Open the Analysis tab

Click the **🔬 Analysis** tab in the Research dock. This is where you choose a template and run the AI extraction.

The document selector at the top of the tab defaults to whichever PDF is currently open in the viewer.

## Step 3 — Choose an analysis template

Select a template from the **mode dropdown**. Each template tells the AI what to look for:

- **Argument Map** — claims, evidence, reasoning chains
- **Methodology Tracker** — research steps and findings
- **Relationship Network** — people, organisations, connections

Start with **Argument Map** if you're not sure — it works well on most academic texts.

## Step 4 — Run the analysis

Click **▶ Run Analysis**. Papyrus splits your document into chunks and sends each to the AI in parallel.

Result cards appear as the AI finishes each chunk, showing the nodes and relationships extracted from that section. For a typical 20-page paper this takes about 30–60 seconds.

## Step 5 — Explore the results

Each **result card** shows how many claims, quotes, and relationships were found in that chunk. Click a card to expand it and read the individual extractions.

- Click **View Prompt Trace** on any card to see exactly what was sent to the AI.
- Click **Send to Workspace** to add those nodes to the visual Workspace canvas.

When you're done reviewing, switch to the **Review & Synthesise** sub-tab to see a master summary across all chunks.

## Chat with your documents

The **💬 Chat** tab lets you have a multi-turn conversation with an AI that has access to all your project documents.

Open the Research dock and click the **💬 Chat** tab to begin.

## Ask your first question

Type a question in the input field at the bottom of the Chat tab and press **Enter** (or click **Send**).

Be specific for best results. Instead of *"Tell me about climate change"*, try *"What arguments do the authors make about carbon pricing in the 2023 papers?"*

The AI response streams in word-by-word.

## Read the citation bubbles

Notice the **citation bubbles** inline in the AI's response. Each one shows:
- The source document name
- The page number
- A short quote of the relevant passage

Click a citation bubble to jump directly to that page in the PDF viewer. This lets you verify the AI's answer against the original source.

## Control which documents the AI uses

By default the AI searches all your documents. To focus it on specific PDFs, click the **⚙️ Settings** button next to the input field.

The **Context Filter** dialog lets you:
- Select specific documents to include
- Filter by tags (using AND or OR logic)

Useful when you want the AI to compare just two papers, or only look at documents tagged with a particular topic.

## See what was sent to the AI

Every AI response includes a **View Prompt Trace** button (look for it on the response card). Click it to open the Trace Viewer, which shows:

- The exact system prompt used
- The document chunks retrieved by RAG
- Token usage
- The raw model response

This is essential for understanding *why* the AI gave a particular answer.

## Highlighting text

Open a PDF in the viewer and select any text by clicking and dragging. Then **right-click** the selection.

A context menu appears. Hover over **Highlight** to see the five colour options:
- 🟡 Yellow, 🟢 Green, 🔵 Blue, 🟣 Purple, 🔴 Red

Click a colour to apply the highlight. It is saved immediately and appears in the Notes dock.

## Adding a note to a highlight

Click any highlight to select it. A text field appears — type your note there and press **Enter** to save.

Your note is now attached to that highlighted passage.

## The Notes dock

All your highlights and notes are collected in the **Notes dock** (open it from Toolbar → Other Tools → Notes List).

Each note card shows:
- The source document and page number
- The highlighted text
- Your note
- Colour picker buttons to change the colour
- A **✖** delete button

Use the **Scope** dropdown to switch between *Current PDF* and *Entire Project*.

## Tagging highlights

Right-click any highlight (in the PDF viewer or the Notes dock) and choose **Manage Tags** to assign tags.

Once tagged, you can filter the Notes dock and the Document Explorer to show only highlights with a particular tag — useful for grouping all "counterargument" or "key statistic" highlights across many documents.

## The Knowledge Workspace

The **Workspace** is a visual canvas where extracted knowledge lives as a graph of nodes (ideas, claims, entities) connected by edges (relationships).

Open the Workspace dock now — look for the Workspace button in the toolbar or side panel.

## Navigating the canvas

Try these controls:
- **Scroll** — zoom in and out
- **Middle-click drag** (or two-finger swipe) — pan the canvas
- **Click a node** — select it and view its details
- **Double-click a node** — open the full node editor

If the canvas is empty, run an analysis first (🔬 Analysis tab → Run Analysis → Send to Workspace).

## Connecting nodes manually

You can draw your own relationships between nodes:
1. Hover over a node until a small **port circle** appears on its edge.
2. Click and drag from the port to another node.
3. Choose a relationship type from the dialog that appears.

You can also right-click the canvas and choose **Add Node** to create a node from scratch.

## AI tools on your graph

Right-click the canvas to access AI workspace tools:

- **Find Weakpoints** — identifies unsupported claims (nodes with no evidence edges)
- **Color Organise by Theme** — clusters nodes by topic and recolours them
- **Generate Outline** — creates a hierarchical text outline from selected nodes
- **Declutter & Simplify** — merges duplicates and removes noise

Try **Color Organise by Theme** after importing a large analysis to instantly see how topics cluster.

## Multiple workspaces

The **dropdown at the top of the Workspace dock** lets you switch between named workspaces. You start with a **Main Board**.

Click **+ New Workspace** to create a separate canvas for a different aspect of your research — for example, one for "argument structure" and another for "key people and organisations".

You're all set! The Workspace is your research thinking space — build it up over time.

## Brainstorm tab

The **💡 Brainstorm** tab generates ideas, arguments, and hypotheses by synthesising your documents with AI reasoning.

Open the Research dock and click the **💡 Brainstorm** tab.

## Choose a strategy

The **strategy dropdown** controls how much the AI relies on your documents:

- **Creative Synthesis** — free ideation, loosely inspired by your docs
- **RAG + Creative Expansion** — grounded in documents, then expands creatively
- **Strict Document Evidence Only** — only uses what's directly in your documents

For generating new ideas, start with **Creative Synthesis**. For evidence-based summaries, use **Strict Document Evidence Only**.

## Write a brainstorm prompt

Type a directive — not a question — and click **Send**. Examples:

- *"Generate 5 research hypotheses based on the patterns in these papers."*
- *"List the strongest counterarguments to the privatisation of public services."*
- *"Compare how different authors frame the concept of resilience."*

Results stream in with numbered ideas and inline citations from your documents.

## The Research Agent

The **🧭 Research Agent** tab is an autonomous AI that can perform multi-step research on your behalf — planning a strategy, running searches, synthesising results, and checking back with you at key moments.

Open the Research dock and click the **🧭 Research Agent** tab.

## State a research goal

Type a specific, outcome-oriented goal in the input field. The more specific you are, the better:

**Good**: *"Find the 3 strongest empirical arguments against low-carb diets in my documents, cite the studies, and list any methodological weaknesses each argument has."*

**Too vague**: *"Tell me about diets."*

Click **▶ Start** when ready.

## Review the plan

The agent first shows you its **plan** — a list of steps it intends to take. Read through it and decide:

- If the plan looks good, click **Continue** to let it proceed.
- If you want to redirect it, type a new instruction in the input field — for example: *"Skip step 2 and focus on step 3 only."*

The **Status Pill** at the top shows: Idle → Planning → Executing as it works.

## Step results and artifacts

After each step, the agent reports what it found as an **artifact** card — a summary, a set of quotes, a comparison, etc.

Review the artifact, then:
- Click **Continue** to move to the next step.
- Type a correction or addition in the input field to adjust direction.
- Click **New** to abandon this session and start fresh.

The session is saved in your project — if you close Papyrus, you can resume later.

## Blueprint Editor

The **🛠️ Blueprint Editor** is where you build reusable AI workflows — called **blueprints** — by connecting action nodes.

Open the Research dock and click the **🛠️ Blueprint Editor** tab. You'll see a node canvas on the left and a two-tab panel on the right (AI Builder and Debugger).

## Create a new tool

Click the **✨ New Tool** button at the top of the editor. This clears the canvas and prepares a blank blueprint.

Give your tool a name in the **Name** field at the bottom of the editor. For example: *"Summarise Key Arguments"*.

## Add a RAG Search node

Click **+ Add Node** and select **RAG Search**. Configure it:
- **Query**: `{user_input}` — this passes the user's typed query to the search
- **Max chunks**: 5
- **Output variable**: `rag_results`

This node will search your documents for passages relevant to whatever the user types.

## Add an LLM Query node

Click **+ Add Node** and select **LLM Query**. Configure it:
- **Prompt**: `"Based on the following passages from my research documents, identify and summarise the key arguments about '{user_input}':\n\n{rag_results}\n\nFormat the output as a numbered list."`
- **Output variable**: `summary`

Then connect the RAG Search node's output to this node's input by dragging between the nodes.

## Test in the Debugger

Switch to the **Debugger** tab in the right panel. Click **Run Test in Debugger**.

The debugger walks through each node step-by-step, showing the full state dictionary after each one. You'll see `rag_results` filled in after the search, then `summary` filled in after the LLM node.

If a step fails, the error appears in the terminal output below.

## Save your blueprint

Click **Save Blueprint** in the bottom bar. Your new tool is now available in the **🧰 Custom Tools** tab.

Switch to the Custom Tools tab, select your tool from the dropdown, type a topic in the input field, and click **▶ Run Tool** to use it any time.

title: Create a Custom Tool with the AI Builder

steps.text:
## AI Builder — describe your workflow

Instead of building a blueprint node by node, you can **describe** what you want and let the AI build it for you.

Open the Blueprint Editor (🛠️ tab in the Research dock) and click the **AI Builder** tab in the right panel.

## Describe what you want

Type a plain-English description of your workflow. Be specific about inputs, steps, and the desired output. For example:

> *"Let the user type a research question. Search my documents for relevant passages. Then write a 3-paragraph essay answering the question, citing the retrieved passages inline."*

Click **Send**. The AI generates the blueprint and renders it on the canvas in real time.

## Refine with follow-up messages

Review the generated nodes on the canvas. If anything needs changing, just describe the modification in the chat:

- *"Make the essay 5 paragraphs instead of 3."*
- *"Add a step that first extracts the 5 most relevant quotes before writing the essay."*
- *"Change the output to bullet points."*

The AI updates the blueprint immediately with each instruction.

## Save and run

When satisfied, enter a name in the **Name** field at the bottom and click **Save Blueprint**.

Switch to the **🧰 Custom Tools** tab to run it. Any `expected_inputs` you declared appear as a form — fill them in and click **▶ Run Tool**.

## What is Prompt Trace?

**Prompt Trace** shows you the exact prompt sent to the AI model for any response — including the system instructions, the document chunks retrieved by RAG, the variables injected, token usage, and the raw model output.

This tutorial shows you how to access it after a Chat or Analysis response.

## Finding the Prompt Trace button

After any AI response — in Chat, Analysis results, or Custom Tool output — look for the **View Prompt Trace** button on the response card.

In the Chat tab, it may appear when you hover over a message. In the Analysis tab, it appears on each chunk result card.

Click **View Prompt Trace** now on any response you've already received.

## Reading the Trace Viewer

The **Trace Viewer** dialog opens showing:

- **System prompt** — the role and instructions given to the AI
- **Retrieved chunks** — the exact document passages included in this call
- **User message** — what was sent as the user turn
- **Token usage** — prompt tokens, completion tokens
- **Raw response** — the model's unprocessed output

Use this to understand *why* the AI gave a particular answer — or to diagnose problems.

## Improving prompts

If you see something in the trace you want to improve — for example, the system prompt is too generic — open the **Prompt Editor** (🧠 in the toolbar).

Select the relevant prompt key, make your edits, and click **Save**. The next AI call will use the updated prompt. Use Prompt Trace again to verify the change was applied.
Open the Blueprint Editor by clicking the Blueprint Editor tab in the Research Assistant dock on the right side of the screen.
Click '+ New Blueprint' at the top of the Blueprint Editor to create a new blank workflow. Give it a name like 'My First Blueprint'.
In the left sidebar, click 'RAG Search' under the Search category. This adds a document search step to the canvas. It will search your indexed documents for relevant context.

Click the RAG Search node on the canvas to select it. In the Inspector panel (right side), set the Query/Input field to '{user_input}' — this tells the step to use whatever the user types when running the blueprint. Set N Results to 5.

Click 'LLM Query' in the sidebar to add an AI response step. Set its System Prompt to something like: 'You are a research assistant. Answer based on the provided context.' Set its Query/Input to '{rag_results}' (the output key from the RAG step).
Click the RAG Search node, then Ctrl+click the LLM Query node to select both. Click 'Connect Selected' — this creates a Sequence edge so the RAG step runs first and passes its output to the LLM.

Under 'GUI Output Nodes' in the sidebar, click 'Live Text'. This adds an output node. Select the LLM Query node and the Live Text node, then click Connect Selected — this renders the AI response as streaming text.
In the Mount Points field at the top, type 'custom_tools_tab' to make this blueprint appear in the Custom Tools tab. You can add more locations like 'notes_dock' or 'data_dock' separated by commas.
Click 'Save Blueprint'. Then switch to the right panel's Debugger tab and click 'Run Test in Debugger' to test your pipeline. You'll see each step's output in the debug log.
